newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania awaits foreign troops after Italian vote.
newsitem.headline: Albania awaits foreign troops after Italian vote.

text.p: Chaotic Albania looked forward to the arrival of foreign troops within days, after Rome's parliament cleared the way for the Italian-led, multinational mission.

Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said his emergency all-party government could begin focusing on fighting organised crime in the country, racked by weeks of violence, once the U.N.-backed security force arrives early next week.

Fino said in an interview with Reuters the 6,000-man contingent was needed to secure Albania's main ports and airport while giving the emergency government time to reorganise its scattered, demoralised security forces.

"The presence of these forces is very important for us because, in this difficult situation, our police are reorganising," said Fino, who added Albania was sending letters of thanks to Italy's upper and lower houses.
"Our police will thus have the chance to better focus on fighting against organised crime."
The troops from Italy, France, Spain, Turkey, Greece and Romania are expected to start arriving on Monday and will protect the delivery of emergency food and medical supplies.
About two dozen military experts from those countries had already arrived in Tirana by Wednesday to prepare the mission.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi won support late on Wednesday to send Italian troops to Albania but at the cost of a rift with his hard left allies that will expose his government to a confidence test in parliament.
Prodi staved off an immediate government crisis when the centre-right opposition said it would support a joint motion on the Albania force, whose deployment is expected next week.

Albania, Europe's poorest country, plunged into near-chaos when get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes failed and armed rebels took control of the south during an unchecked spasm of looting and banditry.

More than 200 people have been killed and about 700 injured in the violence. Army arsenals were looted after soldiers and police abandoned their posts and thousands of automatic rifles and other weapons were seized by citizens who brandished them on the streets.
A strictly enforced 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew has restored a semblance of order to the capital and surrounding area, but many regions are still viewed as lawless.

Albania's main opposition Socialist Party returned to parliament on Wednesday nearly a year after it abandoned its seats charging widespread election fraud. The leftist party agreed to drop its boycott of the parliament in a bid to help rebuild confidence and restore order.
As the Socialists said they were prepared to cooperate with President Sali Berisha, the embattled rightist leader blamed others for the country's turmoil.
In an interview published in Thursday's edition of a Vienna weekly magazine News, Berisha was quoted using unusually blunt language in blaming the Socialists for the mayhem.

"The Socialists have pushed us into this situation. They spread hatred, acted like bandits, excluded themselves from political life in Albania. Their style created the climate of intolerance that has now led to the explosion."
Fino, Albania's 34-year-old prime minister and a leader of the leftist Socialist party, told Reuters he had no plans to respond to Berisha's criticism.

"He can speak with this tongue," Fino said. "Currently we don't intend to speak with the same language because we want to convey the message of peace, understanding and reconciliation to our people. The softer one speaks, the more the ballot boxes will be filled with free votes."
Albania's exiled king, who has spent only a few days of his life in his Balkan homeland, plans to return in an effort to help calm the turmoil there, a monarchist party leader said.

Guri Durollari of the Legality Movement party said King Leka I, who lives in South Africa, was planning to fly to Albania on Saturday. Leka Zogu, 58, was only a few days old when his father, King Zog, fled the country with his family in 1939.

The parliament lifted press restrictions which the all-party government introduced last month. The emergency measure had required all Albanian newspapers to submit articles in advance of publication to government-appointed committees for approval.
